headline: UK police to get medical cannabis training in February 2027
dek: The author of UK police guidance on medical cannabis patients plans an online course for officers in February 2027 and a second edition that adds driving advice.
key_points: Richard List, national secretary of the Association of Police Controlled Drug Liaison Officers, is organising a national online event for officers on medical cannabis in February 2027, Cannabis Health reported on 20 November.

His guidance, Patient First, Suspect Second, was approved by the National Police Chiefs' Council in October 2025 and tells officers to treat a self-declared patient as a patient unless shown otherwise.
A second edition will add driving guidance agreed with the NPCC roads policing lead, but it awaits specialist legal advice and has no publication date.
Patients are not legally required to show documents; the guidance accepts a prescription, a specialist's letter or labelled packaging, but not the CanCard.
body: Police officers in the UK are to be offered their first national training session on medical cannabis in February 2027. Richard List, the retired senior detective who wrote the national guidance on how officers should treat medical cannabis patients, told Cannabis Health in an interview published on 20 November that he is organising an online event with the Association of Police Controlled Drug Liaison Officers (APCDLO), where he is national secretary. It will cover what prescribed cannabis is and how to check that someone is a patient, and it will be recorded.

List also confirmed that the second edition of his guidance will include advice on driving, the area where patients say they are treated most unevenly. That edition has been agreed with the National Police Chiefs' Council's roads policing portfolio, but a briefing paper has gone for specialist legal advice first, and he said it will take some time. No date has been set.

List speaks with some authority inside policing. He is a former detective chief superintendent with 30 years' service, including leading the Thames Valley Police drug squad, and he now holds the national secretary post at the APCDLO, an association of police officers who specialise in controlled drugs. The guidance he wrote is national, but each force decides how to brief its own officers, which is why a single recorded training session matters.

The guidance, titled Patient First, Suspect Second, was published in October 2025 and approved by the National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC). Its core instruction is that an officer who meets someone saying they are a medical cannabis patient should treat them as a patient until shown otherwise.

It lists three acceptable forms of evidence: the prescription, on paper or digital; a letter from the specialist prescriber; or the pharmacy packaging, which should carry the patient's details. A patient card issued by the Releaf clinic is not in the first edition but will be in the second. The CanCard, a card sold to patients as proof of status, is not an approved form of verification and does not show lawful possession, List told the outlet.

Patients are not legally obliged to produce any of this, because of medical confidentiality. The Department of Health and Social Care and clinics still advise patients to carry something that identifies them as a patient.
> The UK legalised the prescription in 2018. It has taken until 2027 to start training the officers who meet the patients.

Driving is where the first edition is thinnest. It gives only basic advice on impairment, List said. Two offences apply. One, under section 4 of the Road Traffic Act 1988, covers driving while impaired by drugs. The other, under section 5A, introduced in 2015, sets a limit of 2 micrograms of THC per litre of blood, a level Cannabis Health says most patients on prescribed cannabis exceed. Patients report that roadside responses vary from force to force.

Until the new edition appears, List's advice to patients is simple: do not drive if you feel impaired in any way. That leaves the central question for patients, how an officer at the roadside should treat a prescribed patient above the limit who shows no impairment, without a national answer for now.
## Why it matters to the market

The route to a prescription is getting more mainstream. As we reported on 16 November, Boots has launched a private medical cannabis service, the first from a high-street pharmacy chain. Every new patient is a potential roadside or street encounter, so how officers treat patients matters to the market's growth.

For clinics, pharmacies and producers, a recognised national standard on verification and driving would remove a practical barrier to growth. The guidance does that only in part. Its verification rules are clear, but it has no statutory force, and with 43 territorial police forces to reach, how quickly it reaches the officer on the street depends on training of the kind List is now organising.

List speaks at the Cannabis Health London Symposium at Conway Hall on Thursday 26 November. Watch for a date for the February 2027 training event and for the outcome of the legal advice on driving, which will decide what the second edition can say. Watch, too, whether the Releaf card's inclusion prompts other clinics to seek recognition for their own patient cards.
